title: Elizabeth of the Trinity (1880–1906)
hook: a young Carmelite who found heaven, she said, inside her own soul

segments.voice: Yesterday, roses: Thérèse's promise to keep doing good after she was gone. Your line was heaven doing good. Did your unsigned kindness find its way to someone? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

Heaven on earth. People say it about a beach at sunset, a first apartment, a plate of really good pasta. A young Carmelite in the French city of Dijon used the same phrase in a letter, and meant something stranger. She wrote that she had found her heaven on earth, because heaven is God, and God is in the soul. Not a place to get to someday. A presence already home. Her name in Carmel was Elizabeth of the Trinity, and today she is our word.
screen: `HEAVEN ON EARTH.` → `A LETTER FROM DIJON.` → `GOD ALREADY HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the promise she built on. In John's Gospel, at the Last Supper, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any one love me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and will make our abode with him." We will come. Father and Son, and Christian teaching adds the Spirit with them: the Trinity, not visiting but moving in. Elizabeth took that verse literally. Her whole spiritual life was learning to live with the guests already inside. Second, her prayer. She wrote a prayer to the Trinity that begins, in English versions, O my God, Trinity whom I adore. In it she asks to forget herself entirely, to be settled in God as still and peaceful as if her soul were already in eternity, and to let nothing draw her out. It isn't a prayer of requests. It's a prayer of staying put. Third, her new name. Reading Saint Paul's letter to the Ephesians, she found a phrase about Christians being made "unto the praise of his glory." She took it, in Latin, as a name for herself: Laudem Gloriae, praise of glory. She wanted her life to be one long act of praise, even in the illness that ended it young. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary afternoon. Elizabeth's idea is not that God is far away and we must climb. It's that God is nearer than the next thought, and prayer is turning around to notice. The Church later declared her a saint. Her prayer is still prayed in Carmels and in kitchens.
screen: `WE WILL COME TO HIM.` · `A PRAYER OF STAYING PUT.` · `LAUDEM GLORIAE: PRAISE OF GLORY.` · then, large: `GOD NEARER THAN THE NEXT THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray to God within. Settle, and breathe. Instead of sending your attention up, or out, let it sink down, behind the breastbone, beneath the busy thoughts. Elizabeth pictured her soul as a quiet home with guests already there. You don't need to make anything happen. Just turn toward that inner room and stay. When a thought pulls you out, come back in, gently. If you pray, you can say the verse slowly: we will come to him, and make our abode with him. If you don't, simply rest in the stillest place you can find inside. The bell holds the time.
Elizabeth of the Trinity. A Carmelite of Dijon who prayed to the Trinity dwelling within, and called herself praise of glory. Today's word.

Your line: the trinity within. Three times today, in a doorway, a checkout line, a red light, turn inward for one breath and notice who might already be home. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics who follow Elizabeth of the Trinity pray her prayer to the Trinity, often in quiet before the Blessed Sacrament or at home, and use John 14:23 as a doorway into silent prayer.
